question: On a multiwire branch circuit in a 120/240V panel, the two hots must be:
choices: On the same leg so the neutral cancels
On opposite legs, with a means to disconnect them together
On any two breakers, neutral size does not matter
Separated by at least four panel spaces
explain_plain: Opposite legs keep the shared neutral carrying only unbalanced current, and the hots must be disconnectable together.

question: A 240V dryer receptacle in a dwelling laundry area needs GFCI protection in NEC 2020 because:
choices: 210.8(A) covers 125V through 250V receptacles, and laundry areas are item (10)
Only the washer receptacle needs it
explain_plain: The 2020 voltage range plus the laundry-area item is the whole point; the dryer is not exempt for being 240V.

question: Which of these is on the NEC 2020 non-dwelling GFCI list in 210.8(B)?
choices: A rooftop receptacle on an office building
explain_plain: Rooftops are a named non-dwelling location. The dwelling list in 210.8(A) does not govern an office roof.

question: AFCI protection under 210.12(A) applies in dwellings to branch circuits that are:
choices: 120V, single-phase, 15A or 20A, supplying outlets or devices in listed rooms
explain_plain: Those rating limits, plus the room list, define the subsection. A 240V appliance circuit is outside its stated range.

question: A continuous load of 48A requires a circuit sized at no less than:
explain_plain: 48 x 1.25 = 60A for conductor and overcurrent sizing, absent a listed continuous-rated assembly.

question: A single receptacle on an individual 20A branch circuit must be rated at least:
explain_plain: A single receptacle on an individual circuit must have a rating not less than the circuit rating. 15A duplex devices are permitted on a multi-outlet 20A circuit, which is a different case.

question: An island countertop measures 27 sq ft. Under the NEC 2020 area method in the v1 checklist, it needs at least:
explain_plain: One receptacle for the first 9 sq ft and one more for each additional 18 sq ft or part: 27 sq ft is the first block plus one additional block. See K-03.

question: A new four-bay dwelling garage needs at least how many receptacles under 210.52(G)(1)?
explain_plain: NEC 2020 requires at least one receptacle in each vehicle bay.

question: The HVAC service receptacle required by 210.63 must be:
choices: Within 25 ft of the equipment, on the same level, and not fed from the load side of the equipment disconnect
On the equipment circuit so it dies with the unit
explain_plain: Distance, level, and the line-side connection are the three field checks in 210.63.

question: A feeder carries 80A of noncontinuous load and 40A of continuous load. Its conductors need ampacity of at least:
explain_plain: 80 + (40 x 1.25) = 80 + 50 = 130A before correction and derating.

question: A dwelling is 40 ft by 50 ft outside dimensions. Its general lighting load at 3 VA per sq ft is:
Under 220.82, a dwelling feeder may use the optional method only when:
choices: The house is over 2,000 sq ft
The feeder carries the entire load of the dwelling and the other conditions of the section are met
explain_plain: The entire-load condition is what makes the demand factors legitimate; a partial feeder is calculated by the standard method.

question: An optional-method general-load total, before heating and cooling, is 22 kVA. The demand-factored general load is:
explain_plain: First 10 kVA at 100% = 10 kVA; remaining 12 kVA at 40% = 4.8 kVA; total 14.8 kVA. This uses only the 220.82(B) demand step already carried in checked table 220.82.

question: A detached barn already has one feeder. Running a second ordinary feeder to it is:
choices: Fine if each has its own breaker
Generally not permitted; one supply, apart from the exceptions 225.30 lists
Fine if the conductors are larger
explain_plain: One supply is the general rule. Convenience is not one of the listed exceptions, and any exception used needs a directory plaque.

question: Power fed to a separate building must have, at that building:
choices: A disconnecting means as Article 225 requires
Nothing, the main building breaker is enough
explain_plain: The building being supplied gets its own disconnect, grouped and rated as the article's following sections require.

question: NEC 2020 requires a dwelling service to have:
choices: A Type 1 or Type 2 surge protective device in or next to the service equipment
A surge strip at the TV
A Type 3 device at every receptacle
explain_plain: 230.67, new in 2020, puts a Type 1 or Type 2 SPD at the service equipment. Point-of-use strips do not satisfy it.

question: Under the NEC 2020 arrangement in 230.71, each service disconnect must be:
choices: In the same enclosure as all the others
In its own enclosure, grouped as the section requires
Limited to one per building in all cases
explain_plain: The 2020 reorganization requires separate enclosures for separate service disconnects, up to the stated maximum, grouped as required.

question: A house has a calculated load of 132A. The minimum service disconnect rating is governed by:
choices: The 100A floor in 230.79(C), so 100A is plenty
The Article 220 calculation, so the service must cover 132A
The size of the old service
explain_plain: 100A is only a floor. A calculation above it controls, and the service is sized to the calculated load.

question: A feeder conductor has 90A ampacity and is not part of a receptacle branch circuit. Using 240.4(B), its protection may be:
choices: The next higher standard rating, 100A, if every condition in 240.4(B) is met
explain_plain: Next-higher is an allowance with conditions, including the ceiling stated in the subsection, which 90A ampacity and a 100A device are within.

question: The maximum overcurrent protection for 10 AWG copper-clad aluminum on a general branch circuit is:
explain_plain: 240.4(D) caps 10 AWG aluminum and CCA at 25A — tighter than 10 AWG copper at 30A, and the reason CCA goes one size up under S-10.

question: Which of these is NOT a standard rating listed in 240.6(A)?
explain_plain: 45A, 60A, and 175A are standard steps; 52A is a calculated value, not a standard device rating.

question: A ground rod alone will clear a 20A ground fault by:
choices: Carrying fault current through the earth back to the source
It will not; earth is not an effective fault-current path, and the bonded equipment grounding path does that job
Raising the voltage until the breaker opens
explain_plain: 250.4 is explicit that earth is not the fault-clearing path. Bonding back to the source is.

question: In a subpanel fed from a house service, the correct arrangement is:
choices: Bond neutral to the can so faults clear
Neutral isolated from the can; equipment grounds bonded to the can
Neutral and grounds landed together on one bar
explain_plain: The bond lives at the service only. Downstream, neutrals float and grounds bond to the enclosure.

question: A new feeder to a detached garage is run. At the garage you must provide:
choices: A re-bonded neutral and no rods
Its own grounding electrode system, an equipment ground run with the feeder, and an isolated neutral
Only two rods, no equipment ground
explain_plain: 250.32 gives the separate building electrodes plus a feeder equipment ground, with the bond left at the service.

question: One ground rod measures 30 ohms to earth and no test record supports anything better. The installation needs:
choices: A supplemental electrode, typically a second rod at least 6 ft away
explain_plain: A single rod must show 25 ohms or less or be supplemented. 30 ohms does not meet it.

question: Service conductors are 4/0 copper. Table 250.66 gives a copper grounding electrode conductor of:
explain_plain: 4/0 is larger than 3/0, so it falls in the next row up from the 2/0-or-3/0 row: over 3/0 through 350 kcmil copper service conductors take a 2 AWG copper GEC. The trap is stopping one row early at 4 AWG, which is the answer for 2/0 or 3/0.

question: A circuit's conductors are upsized from 12 AWG to 8 AWG for voltage drop. The equipment grounding conductor must be:
choices: Increased in proportion to the circular-mil increase of the circuit conductors
Removed, because larger wire runs cooler
explain_plain: 250.122(B) ties the ground's increase to the conductors' increase, by circular-mil proportion.

question: Copper-clad aluminum (CCA) branch-circuit wire gets its ampacity from which column of Table 310.16?
choices: Its own CCA column printed in the table
The 90°C column, whatever the cable type
explain_plain: CCA sizes like aluminum — rate it in the aluminum column at the cable's temperature limit, then apply the 240.4(D) caps.

question: A 20A kitchen small-appliance circuit is wired in CCA NM cable. The smallest permitted conductor is:
explain_plain: 240.4(D) caps 12 AWG CCA at 15A, so a 20A circuit takes 10 AWG CCA — one size up from copper.

question: Two identical boxes hold the same count of 12 AWG THHN conductors, one run in copper and one in CCA. The required box volume is:
choices: The same — 314.16(B) is figured by conductor size and insulation, not by the metal
Zero, because fill only counts copper
explain_plain: Box fill goes by AWG size and insulation type; the conductor metal never enters the calculation.

question: Which termination is permitted for a CCA conductor?
choices: A push-in (backstab) terminal on a receptacle
An unmarked lug, torqued extra tight to compensate
explain_plain: Standard 15/20A device screw terminals accept CCA; splice connectors must be marked for the conductor (AL/CU), and backstab terminals are listed for 14 AWG solid copper only.
